CHAPTER 7 - SHOOT SYSTEM

Introduction

A flowering plant (angiosperm) has two main parts - the ROOT SYSTEM, which grows downward into the soil, and the SHOOT SYSTEM, which grows upward into the air. The shoot system develops from the plumule of the germinating embryo and consists of the STEM together with all the structures it bears - the LEAVES, the BUDS, and, when the plant matures, the FLOWERS and FRUITS. Because it grows against gravity (it is negatively geotropic) and towards light (positively phototropic), the shoot displays the plant to the Sun and air. This chapter describes the external and internal structure of the stem and the leaf, the many ways in which each organ is modified to perform special jobs, and the important functions they carry out - above all support, conduction, photosynthesis and transpiration.

7.1 THE STEM AND ITS FEATURES

The STEM is the ascending (upward-growing) axis of the plant that develops from the plumule. It bears leaves, buds, flowers and fruits, and it links the leaves (where food is made) with the roots (where water and minerals are absorbed). A young stem is usually green and photosynthetic; an older stem becomes woody and brown.

Characteristic features of a stem:
- It is generally erect and grows away from the soil, upward towards light.
- It bears NODES and INTERNODES. A NODE is the point on the stem from which one or more leaves arise. The portion of stem between two successive nodes is an INTERNODE. The presence of nodes and internodes is the surest way to tell a stem from a root, because roots have neither.
- It bears BUDS. A bud is a compact, undeveloped (embryonic) shoot. A TERMINAL (apical) bud sits at the tip of the stem and is responsible for growth in length. AXILLARY (lateral) buds occur in the axils - the angle between the leaf base and the stem - and grow out into branches or flowers. Buds may be VEGETATIVE (giving leafy branches) or FLORAL (giving flowers).
- Young stems are usually green because they contain chlorophyll and can photosynthesise.
- The stem branches to spread out the leaves for maximum exposure to sunlight.
- Stems are positively phototropic (bend towards light) and negatively geotropic (grow against gravity).

Functions of the stem: it SUPPORTS and holds up the leaves, flowers and fruits; it CONDUCTS water and minerals upward from the root to the leaves (through the xylem) and carries manufactured food from the leaves to all other parts (through the phloem); green stems help in PHOTOSYNTHESIS; some stems STORE food and water; and modified stems help in vegetative PROPAGATION, climbing, protection and other special tasks.

7.2 INTERNAL STRUCTURE OF DICOT AND MONOCOT STEMS

When a young stem is cut across and viewed under a microscope, its tissues are seen arranged in concentric zones from the outside inwards. The arrangement differs between a DICOTYLEDONOUS (dicot) stem and a MONOCOTYLEDONOUS (monocot) stem, and these differences are a favourite point of comparison.

INTERNAL STRUCTURE OF A YOUNG DICOT STEM (for example, sunflower):
- EPIDERMIS: the outermost single layer of cells, covered by a waterproof CUTICLE and bearing a few stomata and sometimes hairs (trichomes). It protects the inner tissues and checks water loss.
- HYPODERMIS: a few layers lying just below the epidermis, made of COLLENCHYMA (cells with thickened corners). It gives mechanical strength and flexibility to the young green stem.
- CORTEX: several layers of thin-walled PARENCHYMA below the hypodermis; the outer cortical cells may contain chloroplasts and help in photosynthesis and storage.
- ENDODERMIS: the innermost layer of the cortex; its cells are often rich in starch grains, so it is also called the STARCH SHEATH.
- PERICYCLE: a layer of sclerenchyma (and parenchyma) lying inside the endodermis, capping the vascular bundles and giving support.
- VASCULAR BUNDLES: arranged in a RING around the central pith. Each bundle is CONJOINT (xylem and phloem lie in the same bundle), COLLATERAL (phloem lies on the outer side and xylem on the inner side), and OPEN (a strip of CAMBIUM lies between the xylem and phloem). Because the cambium can divide and add new tissue, the dicot stem is capable of SECONDARY GROWTH (increase in girth).
- PITH: the large central region of parenchyma that stores food and water; strips of pith between the vascular bundles are the MEDULLARY RAYS, which conduct materials radially.

INTERNAL STRUCTURE OF A YOUNG MONOCOT STEM (for example, maize):
- EPIDERMIS: a single outer layer with a thick cuticle and few stomata.
- HYPODERMIS: made of SCLERENCHYMA (thick, lignified cells) that gives rigidity.
- GROUND TISSUE: the monocot stem has no clear distinction into cortex, endodermis, pericycle and pith. Instead there is a continuous mass of parenchyma called the GROUND TISSUE in which the bundles are embedded.
- VASCULAR BUNDLES: SCATTERED throughout the ground tissue (not in a ring). They are numerous, and each is CONJOINT, COLLATERAL and CLOSED (there is NO cambium between the xylem and phloem). Because there is no cambium, the monocot stem shows LITTLE or NO secondary growth. Each bundle is surrounded by a BUNDLE SHEATH of sclerenchyma, and in the xylem a water-containing cavity (the protoxylem lacuna or water cavity) is often seen.

SUMMARY OF DICOT VS MONOCOT STEM: the dicot stem has vascular bundles in a RING, bundles are OPEN (with cambium), and shows secondary growth; a distinct cortex, endodermis (starch sheath) and pith are present. The monocot stem has vascular bundles SCATTERED in ground tissue, bundles are CLOSED (no cambium), and shows no secondary growth; a bundle sheath surrounds each bundle. Both have conjoint, collateral bundles with phloem outside and xylem inside.

7.3 STEM MODIFICATIONS

Although a typical stem is an erect green aerial axis, in many plants the stem is MODIFIED (changed in form) to perform a special function such as storage, perennation (surviving unfavourable seasons), vegetative propagation, climbing, protection or even photosynthesis. Modified stems keep the defining features of a stem - nodes, internodes, buds and scale leaves - which is how we recognise them as stems and not roots. Stem modifications are grouped as underground, sub-aerial and aerial.

(A) UNDERGROUND STEM MODIFICATIONS (for storage and perennation):
- RHIZOME: a thick, horizontal underground stem growing parallel to the soil surface, bearing nodes, internodes, scale leaves and buds; for example ginger, turmeric and the banana. It stores food and survives the dry season.
- TUBER (stem tuber): the swollen tip of an underground branch that stores food; for example the POTATO. The "eyes" of a potato are nodes bearing axillary buds, proving it is a stem and not a root.
- BULB: a much reduced disc-like stem bearing many fleshy scale leaves that store food, with roots below and a bud in the centre; for example onion and garlic.
- CORM: a short, swollen, vertical underground stem with nodes, scale leaves and buds; for example Colocasia (arvi) and saffron (Crocus).

(B) SUB-AERIAL STEM MODIFICATIONS (for vegetative propagation, mostly spreading horizontally at or just above the soil):
- RUNNER: a slender stem with long internodes that creeps horizontally along the ground, rooting at the nodes and giving new plants; for example grass and Oxalis.
- STOLON: a slender lateral branch that arises from the base of the main stem, arches over and touches the soil to form a new plant; for example strawberry and jasmine.
- OFFSET: a short, thick horizontal branch of one internode that produces a rosette of leaves above and roots below, common in aquatic plants; for example water hyacinth (Eichhornia) and Pistia.
- SUCKER: a lateral branch that arises from the underground base of the stem, grows horizontally beneath the soil and then emerges above ground as a new shoot; for example chrysanthemum, mint (pudina) and pineapple.

(C) AERIAL STEM MODIFICATIONS (above ground, for climbing, protection or photosynthesis):
- STEM TENDRIL: a thin, wiry, coiling branch that helps a weak-stemmed plant to climb by twining around a support; for example grapevine, passion flower and Cucurbita (gourd).
- THORN: a hard, pointed, woody modified axillary branch that protects the plant from grazing animals and may reduce water loss; for example Bougainvillea, Citrus (lemon) and Duranta.
- PHYLLOCLADE: a green, flattened or cylindrical photosynthetic stem of unlimited growth found in xerophytes (desert plants) whose leaves are reduced to spines to save water; for example Opuntia (prickly pear) and Casuarina. A single-internode green stem doing the same job is a CLADODE (for example Asparagus).

7.4 THE LEAF - EXTERNAL STRUCTURE AND VENATION

The LEAF is a flattened, green, lateral outgrowth borne at the node of a stem or branch, in the axil of which lies a bud. It is the chief PHOTOSYNTHETIC organ of the plant. A leaf is exogenous (arises from the surface tissues), has limited growth, and does not bear buds on its surface (unlike a stem).

PARTS OF A TYPICAL LEAF: A typical dicot leaf has three parts.
- LEAF BASE (hypopodium): the part by which the leaf is attached to the stem. In many monocots (grasses) it expands into a sheath around the stem; in legumes it swells into a PULVINUS.
- PETIOLE (mesopodium): the stalk that joins the leaf base to the lamina and holds the blade out in the light. A leaf with a petiole is PETIOLATE; one without is SESSILE.
- LAMINA (leaf blade or epipodium): the broad, green, flattened expanded part where photosynthesis and transpiration take place. The lamina has a prominent central vein, the MIDRIB, from which smaller VEINS and VEINLETS branch. Veins give mechanical support and carry water in and food out. Small leaf-like structures at the leaf base are STIPULES.

VENATION: The arrangement of veins and veinlets in the lamina is called VENATION. There are two main types.
- RETICULATE VENATION: the veinlets form a NET-LIKE (reticulate) pattern between the larger veins. It is typical of DICOT leaves; for example mango, peepal and rose.
- PARALLEL VENATION: the veins run PARALLEL to one another with little cross-linking. It is typical of MONOCOT leaves; for example grass, maize, banana and canna.

TYPES OF LEAVES:
- SIMPLE LEAF: the lamina is a single undivided piece, or if incised the cuts do not reach the midrib; for example mango, guava and peepal.
- COMPOUND LEAF: the lamina is completely divided into several small leaflets, the incisions reaching down to the midrib or petiole. In a PINNATELY compound leaf the leaflets are arranged along a central axis (rachis), as in neem and rose; in a PALMATELY compound leaf the leaflets arise from a common point at the tip of the petiole, as in silk cotton (Bombax). A bud lies in the axil of a whole leaf but NOT in the axil of a leaflet - this distinguishes a compound leaf from a branch bearing simple leaves.

PHYLLOTAXY: The pattern of arrangement of leaves on the stem or branch is called PHYLLOTAXY. Its purpose is to expose every leaf to the maximum sunlight with the least mutual shading. There are three common types.
- ALTERNATE (spiral): a single leaf arises at each node in an alternate manner; for example China rose, mustard and sunflower.
- OPPOSITE: a pair of leaves arises at each node, one against the other. In OPPOSITE DECUSSATE, successive pairs are at right angles (as in Calotropis); in OPPOSITE SUPERPOSED, all pairs lie in one plane (as in guava).
- WHORLED: more than two leaves arise in a whorl (circle) at each node; for example Alstonia and Nerium.

7.5 INTERNAL STRUCTURE OF A LEAF

A vertical section through a leaf blade shows three tissue systems - the epidermis, the mesophyll, and the vascular tissue. The structure differs between a DORSIVENTRAL leaf (a typical dicot leaf, with a distinct upper and lower surface) and an ISOBILATERAL leaf (a typical monocot leaf, with both surfaces alike).

INTERNAL STRUCTURE OF A DORSIVENTRAL (DICOT) LEAF:
- EPIDERMIS: a single layer covers both surfaces. The UPPER epidermis is coated with a thicker cuticle to check water loss and usually has FEWER stomata. The LOWER epidermis has MORE stomata. Each stoma (pore) is bordered by two bean-shaped GUARD CELLS that open and close it, controlling gas exchange and transpiration.
- MESOPHYLL: the green tissue between the two epidermal layers, packed with chloroplasts, where photosynthesis occurs. In a dorsiventral leaf the mesophyll is clearly DIFFERENTIATED into two regions: (i) the PALISADE PARENCHYMA - one or more layers of long, closely packed, cylindrical cells rich in chloroplasts, lying just below the UPPER epidermis, which carry out most of the photosynthesis; and (ii) the SPONGY PARENCHYMA - loosely arranged, irregular cells with large air spaces (intercellular spaces) lying towards the LOWER epidermis, which allow gases to diffuse and connect to the stomata.
- VASCULAR BUNDLES: the veins contain conjoint, collateral, CLOSED bundles with XYLEM towards the upper side and PHLOEM towards the lower side, each surrounded by a BUNDLE SHEATH of parenchyma. The xylem brings water, the phloem carries away the food made in the leaf.

INTERNAL STRUCTURE OF AN ISOBILATERAL (MONOCOT) LEAF:
- EPIDERMIS: present on both surfaces with a thick cuticle; stomata occur on BOTH surfaces in roughly EQUAL numbers. In grasses the upper epidermis bears large, thin-walled BULLIFORM (motor) cells that lose water and fold the leaf during dryness to reduce transpiration.
- MESOPHYLL: NOT differentiated into palisade and spongy layers - it is UNIFORM (undifferentiated) spongy parenchyma with chloroplasts and air spaces throughout.
- VASCULAR BUNDLES: similar conjoint, collateral, closed bundles arranged along the parallel veins, each with a bundle sheath; the bundles are of different sizes corresponding to larger and smaller veins.

SUMMARY OF THE TWO LEAF TYPES: A dorsiventral (dicot) leaf has a differentiated mesophyll (palisade above, spongy below), a thicker upper cuticle, and more stomata on the lower surface. An isobilateral (monocot) leaf has an undifferentiated (uniform) mesophyll, stomata equally on both surfaces, and often bulliform cells; both surfaces look alike.

STOMATA are tiny pores, mostly on the leaf, each guarded by two guard cells. They open and close to control the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide during photosynthesis and respiration, and the escape of water vapour during transpiration.

7.6 LEAF MODIFICATIONS AND FUNCTIONS

Like the stem, the leaf is often MODIFIED to perform functions other than photosynthesis.
- LEAF TENDRILS: the whole leaf or its part becomes a thin coiling tendril for climbing; for example the whole leaf in Lathyrus (wild pea) and leaflet tendrils in pea (Pisum).
- LEAF SPINES: leaves are reduced to hard pointed spines that reduce water loss and give protection; for example the spines of Opuntia and the prickly leaf margins of Argemone (in cacti the stem takes over photosynthesis).
- STORAGE (fleshy) LEAVES: thick fleshy leaves that store food and water; for example the fleshy scale leaves of the onion bulb and the leaves of Aloe.
- LEAF TENDRILS AND HOOKS help climbing; scale leaves protect buds.
- INSECT-CATCHING (insectivorous) LEAVES: in plants growing in nitrogen-poor soils the leaf is modified to trap and digest insects to obtain nitrogen; for example the PITCHER of Nepenthes (pitcher plant), the bladder of Utricularia, and the sensitive lamina of Venus flytrap (Dionaea).
- LEAFLETS OF SOME PLANTS MODIFY INTO TENDRILS while others store water.

FUNCTIONS OF THE LEAF:
- PHOTOSYNTHESIS: the leaf is the main site where green cells use sunlight, carbon dioxide and water to manufacture food (glucose) and release oxygen. Its broad flat lamina, thin structure, abundant chloroplasts and many stomata make it ideally suited for this.
- TRANSPIRATION: the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of the plant, mainly through the stomata of leaves. Transpiration cools the leaf and creates a pull (transpiration pull) that draws water up from the roots.
- GASEOUS EXCHANGE: through the stomata the leaf takes in carbon dioxide and gives out oxygen during photosynthesis, and exchanges gases during respiration.
- STORAGE, PROTECTION, CLIMBING, PROPAGATION and TRAPPING INSECTS by modified leaves as described above; some plants (for example Bryophyllum) even bear buds on the leaf margin for vegetative propagation.

Together the stem and the leaf make up the shoot system that supports the plant, conducts materials, manufactures food and links the plant to its aerial environment.

SUMMARY

- The SHOOT SYSTEM (stem, leaves, buds, flowers) develops from the plumule and grows upward towards light.
- The STEM bears NODES, INTERNODES and BUDS (terminal and axillary); it supports, conducts, and (when green) photosynthesises.
- A DICOT stem has vascular bundles in a RING, bundles conjoint-collateral-OPEN (with cambium) so it shows secondary growth, with distinct cortex, endodermis (starch sheath) and pith. A MONOCOT stem has bundles SCATTERED in ground tissue, conjoint-collateral-CLOSED (no cambium), no secondary growth, each with a bundle sheath.
- STEM MODIFICATIONS: underground (rhizome, tuber, bulb, corm) for storage; sub-aerial (runner, stolon, offset, sucker) for propagation; aerial (tendril, thorn, phylloclade) for climbing, protection and photosynthesis.
- The LEAF has a LEAF BASE, PETIOLE and LAMINA; venation is RETICULATE (dicot) or PARALLEL (monocot); leaves are SIMPLE or COMPOUND; PHYLLOTAXY may be alternate, opposite or whorled.
- A DORSIVENTRAL (dicot) leaf has a differentiated mesophyll (palisade + spongy), thicker upper cuticle and more stomata below; an ISOBILATERAL (monocot) leaf has a uniform mesophyll, stomata on both surfaces and often bulliform cells. STOMATA with guard cells control gas exchange and transpiration.
- LEAF MODIFICATIONS include tendrils, spines, storage leaves and insect-catching leaves.
- The main FUNCTIONS of the shoot are support, conduction, PHOTOSYNTHESIS and TRANSPIRATION.

chapter_summary.intro: This is the NIOS Senior Secondary Biology (314) summary for the Shoot System lesson. It covers the external and internal structure of the stem and the leaf, the arrangement of vascular tissue in dicot and monocot stems, the many modifications of stem and leaf, and the functions of the shoot - support, conduction, photosynthesis and transpiration.

sections.heading: The stem and its features
bullets: The stem is the ascending axis that develops from the plumule and bears leaves, buds, flowers and fruits.
It carries nodes (where leaves arise) and internodes (between nodes); these distinguish a stem from a root.
Buds may be terminal (apical, for growth in length) or axillary (lateral, giving branches or flowers).
Stems support the plant, conduct water, minerals and food, and when green carry out photosynthesis.

sections.heading: Internal structure of dicot and monocot stems
bullets: A dicot stem has, from outside in, epidermis, collenchymatous hypodermis, cortex, endodermis (starch sheath), pericycle, a RING of vascular bundles and central pith.
Dicot bundles are conjoint, collateral and OPEN (cambium present), so the stem shows secondary growth.
A monocot stem has bundles SCATTERED in ground tissue, each with a bundle sheath; the bundles are CLOSED (no cambium), so there is little or no secondary growth.
In both, each bundle is conjoint and collateral with phloem on the outside and xylem on the inside.

sections.heading: Stem modifications
bullets: Underground stems store food and survive bad seasons: rhizome (ginger), stem tuber (potato), bulb (onion) and corm (Colocasia).
Sub-aerial stems spread and propagate: runner (grass), stolon (strawberry), offset (water hyacinth) and sucker (mint).
Aerial stems help in special jobs: stem tendril (grapevine) for climbing, thorn (Citrus) for protection and phylloclade (Opuntia) for photosynthesis in deserts.
Modified stems retain nodes, internodes, scale leaves and buds, which is how they are recognised as stems.

sections.heading: The leaf - external structure and venation
bullets: A typical leaf has a leaf base, a petiole and a broad green lamina with a midrib and veins.
Reticulate (net-like) venation is typical of dicots; parallel venation is typical of monocots.
A simple leaf has an undivided lamina; a compound leaf is divided into leaflets (pinnate or palmate).
Phyllotaxy - the arrangement of leaves - may be alternate, opposite or whorled, arranged to catch maximum light.

sections.heading: Internal structure and functions of the leaf
bullets: A dorsiventral (dicot) leaf has a differentiated mesophyll: palisade parenchyma below the upper epidermis and spongy parenchyma above the lower epidermis, with more stomata on the lower surface.
An isobilateral (monocot) leaf has a uniform (undifferentiated) mesophyll, stomata on both surfaces and often bulliform cells; both surfaces look alike.
Stomata guarded by two guard cells control gaseous exchange and transpiration.
The leaf's chief functions are photosynthesis and transpiration; modified leaves may climb, store food, protect or trap insects.

key_takeaways: The shoot system (stem, leaves, buds, flowers) grows from the plumule and displays the plant to light and air.
Nodes, internodes and buds are the defining features of a stem, present even in modified stems.
A dicot stem has vascular bundles in a ring and is open (with cambium, secondary growth); a monocot stem has scattered, closed bundles (no secondary growth).
Stem modifications are underground (rhizome, tuber, bulb, corm), sub-aerial (runner, stolon, offset, sucker) and aerial (tendril, thorn, phylloclade).
A leaf has a leaf base, petiole and lamina; venation is reticulate in dicots and parallel in monocots; leaves may be simple or compound.
A dorsiventral leaf has palisade and spongy mesophyll and more stomata below; an isobilateral leaf has uniform mesophyll and stomata on both surfaces.
The main functions of the shoot are support, conduction, photosynthesis and transpiration, controlled through stomata.

glossary.definition: The aerial part of a plant - stem, leaves, buds, flowers and fruits - that develops from the plumule and grows towards light.
The point on a stem from which one or more leaves arise; buds occur in the axils of these leaves.
The portion of the stem between two successive nodes.
A compact, undeveloped shoot; a terminal bud lies at the tip and axillary buds in the leaf axils.

A bundle with cambium between xylem and phloem (as in dicot stems), allowing secondary growth.
A bundle without cambium (as in monocot stems), so no secondary growth occurs.

The arrangement of veins in the lamina - reticulate (net-like, dicot) or parallel (monocot).
A leaf whose lamina is completely divided into leaflets, with a bud only in the axil of the whole leaf.
The pattern of arrangement of leaves on a stem - alternate, opposite or whorled - to maximise light capture.
The green photosynthetic tissue of the leaf; differentiated into palisade and spongy layers in a dorsiventral leaf.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Shoot System (NIOS Senior Secondary Biology)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Draw and label diagrams where asked. Give examples wherever possible.

questions.question: Define a node and an internode. Why do these features help us tell a stem apart from a root?
questions.answer: A NODE is the point on a stem from which one or more leaves (and buds in their axils) arise. An INTERNODE is the portion of stem lying between two successive nodes. Roots do not bear leaves and therefore have neither nodes nor internodes, so the presence of nodes and internodes (and buds) is a sure way to identify a structure as a stem rather than a root - even when the stem is modified and lies underground, as in the potato tuber or ginger rhizome.
questions.explanation: Node = leaf-bearing point; internode between nodes; roots lack both.

questions.question: Distinguish between a terminal bud and an axillary bud, giving the function of each.
questions.answer: A TERMINAL (apical) bud is present at the tip of the stem or branch and is responsible for growth in LENGTH of the shoot. An AXILLARY (lateral) bud lies in the axil - the angle between the leaf base and the stem - and grows out into a lateral BRANCH or into a FLOWER. Thus the terminal bud extends the main axis while axillary buds produce branches and flowers.
questions.explanation: Terminal bud = growth in length; axillary bud = branches/flowers.

questions.question: Compare the internal structure of a dicot stem with that of a monocot stem under at least four headings.
questions.answer:
1. VASCULAR BUNDLE ARRANGEMENT: In a dicot stem the vascular bundles are arranged in a RING around the pith; in a monocot stem they are SCATTERED throughout the ground tissue.
2. TYPE OF BUNDLE: In both, bundles are conjoint and collateral (phloem outside, xylem inside), but dicot bundles are OPEN (cambium present between xylem and phloem) while monocot bundles are CLOSED (no cambium).
3. SECONDARY GROWTH: Because the dicot bundle has cambium, the dicot stem shows SECONDARY GROWTH (increase in girth); the monocot stem, lacking cambium, shows LITTLE OR NO secondary growth.
4. GROUND TISSUE: The dicot stem is clearly zoned into cortex, endodermis (starch sheath), pericycle and central pith; in the monocot stem these zones are not distinct and there is a continuous ground tissue with a bundle sheath of sclerenchyma around each bundle.
5. HYPODERMIS: collenchymatous in the dicot stem, sclerenchymatous in the monocot stem.
questions.explanation: Ring vs scattered; open vs closed; secondary growth; zonation; hypodermis.

questions.question: Name the three categories of stem modification and give one example of each.
questions.answer: UNDERGROUND stem modification - example: rhizome of ginger (or potato tuber, onion bulb, Colocasia corm). SUB-AERIAL stem modification - example: runner of grass (or strawberry stolon, water hyacinth offset, mint sucker). AERIAL stem modification - example: stem tendril of grapevine (or Citrus thorn, Opuntia phylloclade).
questions.explanation: Underground, sub-aerial and aerial with one example each.

questions.question: The potato is a stem and not a root. Give two reasons.
questions.answer: (1) The 'eyes' of a potato are NODES that bear axillary BUDS in the axils of scale leaves; buds and scale leaves occur only on stems, not on roots. (2) The potato is the swollen tip of an underground BRANCH (stolon) of the stem and can sprout new shoots from its eyes, which a root cannot do. Therefore the potato tuber is a modified STEM.
questions.explanation: Eyes are nodes with buds and scale leaves - features of a stem.

questions.question: Name the three parts of a typical leaf and state the main job of each.
questions.answer: LEAF BASE: the part attaching the leaf to the stem (it may form a sheath or a pulvinus). PETIOLE: the stalk that holds the lamina out into the light. LAMINA (leaf blade): the broad green flattened part where photosynthesis and transpiration take place, supported and supplied by veins.
questions.explanation: Leaf base (attachment), petiole (stalk/holds blade), lamina (photosynthesis).

questions.question: Differentiate between reticulate and parallel venation and name the plant group each is typical of.
questions.answer: In RETICULATE venation the veinlets form a NET-LIKE pattern between the larger veins; it is typical of DICOT leaves (e.g. mango, peepal). In PARALLEL venation the veins run PARALLEL to one another with little cross-linking; it is typical of MONOCOT leaves (e.g. grass, maize, banana).
questions.explanation: Reticulate = net-like (dicot); parallel = parallel veins (monocot).

questions.question: Describe the internal structure of a dorsiventral (dicot) leaf as seen in vertical section.
questions.answer:
A vertical section of a dorsiventral leaf shows three tissue systems.
(1) EPIDERMIS: a single layer on both surfaces covered by a cuticle. The UPPER epidermis has a thicker cuticle and fewer stomata; the LOWER epidermis has more stomata. Each stoma is bordered by two guard cells.
(2) MESOPHYLL: the green tissue between the epidermal layers, differentiated into two regions - the PALISADE PARENCHYMA of long, closely packed, chloroplast-rich cells just below the upper epidermis (carrying out most photosynthesis), and the SPONGY PARENCHYMA of loosely arranged cells with large air spaces towards the lower epidermis (allowing gas diffusion to the stomata).
(3) VASCULAR BUNDLES: present in the veins, conjoint, collateral and closed, with xylem towards the upper side and phloem towards the lower side, each surrounded by a bundle sheath. Xylem supplies water; phloem removes the food made in the leaf.
questions.explanation: Epidermis (both sides), palisade + spongy mesophyll, vascular bundles.

questions.question: How does an isobilateral (monocot) leaf differ from a dorsiventral (dicot) leaf in its mesophyll and stomata?
questions.answer: In a DORSIVENTRAL (dicot) leaf the mesophyll is DIFFERENTIATED into an upper palisade layer and a lower spongy layer, and stomata are more numerous on the LOWER surface. In an ISOBILATERAL (monocot) leaf the mesophyll is UNIFORM (not differentiated into palisade and spongy), and stomata occur on BOTH surfaces in roughly equal numbers; the leaf often has bulliform (motor) cells in the upper epidermis.
questions.explanation: Differentiated vs uniform mesophyll; stomata below vs on both sides.

questions.question: State any four functions of the leaf and briefly explain photosynthesis and transpiration.
questions.answer: Four functions of the leaf: (1) PHOTOSYNTHESIS, (2) TRANSPIRATION, (3) GASEOUS EXCHANGE, and (4) special jobs by modified leaves (storage, climbing by tendrils, protection by spines or trapping insects). PHOTOSYNTHESIS is the process in which green leaf cells use sunlight, carbon dioxide and water to make food (glucose) and release oxygen; the broad thin lamina, abundant chloroplasts and many stomata suit the leaf for this. TRANSPIRATION is the loss of water vapour from the leaf, mainly through the stomata; it cools the leaf and creates a pull that draws water up from the roots.
questions.explanation: Four functions; photosynthesis = food-making; transpiration = water-vapour loss.

questions.question: What is a stem? From which part of the embryo does it develop?
questions.answer: A STEM is the ascending (upward-growing) axis of the plant that bears leaves, buds, flowers and fruits. It develops from the PLUMULE of the germinating embryo.
questions.explanation: Stem = ascending axis; develops from plumule.

questions.question: List any three characteristic features of a stem.
questions.answer: (1) It bears NODES and INTERNODES. (2) It bears BUDS - a terminal bud at the tip and axillary buds in the leaf axils. (3) It is usually erect, green when young, and grows upward towards light (positively phototropic, negatively geotropic).
questions.explanation: Nodes/internodes, buds, erect green upward growth.

questions.question: State three functions of the stem.
questions.answer: The stem SUPPORTS the leaves, flowers and fruits and holds them up to light; it CONDUCTS water and minerals upward (xylem) and food from the leaves to all parts (phloem); and green stems carry out PHOTOSYNTHESIS. Some stems also store food or help in vegetative propagation.
questions.explanation: Support, conduction, photosynthesis (and storage/propagation).

questions.question: Differentiate between a vegetative bud and a floral bud.
questions.answer: A VEGETATIVE bud develops into a leafy branch or shoot, whereas a FLORAL bud develops into a flower. Both may be terminal or axillary.
questions.explanation: Vegetative bud -> branch; floral bud -> flower.

questions.question: Name the tissue layers of a dicot stem in order from the outside to the centre.
questions.answer: From outside inwards: EPIDERMIS (with cuticle), HYPODERMIS (collenchyma), CORTEX (parenchyma), ENDODERMIS (starch sheath), PERICYCLE, VASCULAR BUNDLES arranged in a ring, and the central PITH with medullary rays.
questions.explanation: Epidermis, hypodermis, cortex, endodermis, pericycle, bundles, pith.

questions.question: What is meant by a conjoint, collateral, open vascular bundle?
questions.answer: CONJOINT means xylem and phloem occur together in the same bundle. COLLATERAL means the phloem lies on the outer side and the xylem on the inner side (they are side by side). OPEN means a strip of cambium is present between the xylem and phloem, allowing secondary growth. This is the bundle type of a dicot stem.
questions.explanation: Conjoint = together; collateral = phloem out/xylem in; open = cambium present.

questions.question: Why is the endodermis of a dicot stem called the starch sheath?
questions.answer: The endodermis is the innermost layer of the cortex, and its cells are usually filled with STARCH grains. Because of this store of starch it is called the STARCH SHEATH.
questions.explanation: Endodermis stores starch grains.

questions.question: What is the role of the cambium in a dicot stem?
questions.answer: The CAMBIUM is a layer of dividing (meristematic) cells lying between the xylem and phloem of an open bundle. By dividing, it adds new secondary xylem and phloem, causing an increase in the girth (thickness) of the stem, i.e. SECONDARY GROWTH.
questions.explanation: Cambium divides to give secondary growth (girth).

questions.question: Explain why a monocot stem shows little or no secondary growth.
questions.answer: In a monocot stem the vascular bundles are CLOSED - there is NO cambium between the xylem and phloem. Since secondary growth (increase in girth) depends on the dividing cambium adding new tissue, and the cambium is absent, the monocot stem shows little or no secondary growth.
questions.explanation: No cambium (closed bundles) -> no secondary growth.

questions.question: Give three differences between a dicot stem and a monocot stem.
questions.answer: (1) Dicot bundles are in a RING; monocot bundles are SCATTERED in the ground tissue. (2) Dicot bundles are OPEN (cambium present); monocot bundles are CLOSED (no cambium). (3) The dicot stem shows secondary growth and has a distinct cortex, endodermis and pith; the monocot stem shows no secondary growth and has ground tissue with a bundle sheath around each bundle.
questions.explanation: Ring vs scattered; open vs closed; secondary growth vs none.

questions.question: State two features common to the vascular bundles of both dicot and monocot stems.
questions.answer: In both, the vascular bundles are (1) CONJOINT (xylem and phloem in the same bundle) and (2) COLLATERAL, with phloem on the outer side and xylem on the inner side.
questions.explanation: Both conjoint and collateral (phloem out, xylem in).

questions.question: Name and give one example each of three types of underground stem modification.
questions.answer: RHIZOME - example ginger; STEM TUBER - example potato; BULB - example onion (a CORM such as Colocasia is a fourth type). These store food and help the plant survive the unfavourable season.
questions.explanation: Rhizome (ginger), tuber (potato), bulb (onion), corm (Colocasia).

questions.question: Differentiate between a runner, a stolon and a sucker.
questions.answer: A RUNNER is a slender stem that creeps along the ground and roots at the nodes to form new plants (e.g. grass). A STOLON is a slender lateral branch that arises from the base, arches over and roots where it touches the soil (e.g. strawberry). A SUCKER arises from the underground base, grows horizontally below the soil and then emerges as a new shoot (e.g. mint). All are sub-aerial stems for vegetative propagation.
questions.explanation: Runner creeps and roots; stolon arches; sucker grows below then emerges.

questions.question: How does a phylloclade help a desert plant survive?
questions.answer: A PHYLLOCLADE is a green, flattened or cylindrical stem that takes over PHOTOSYNTHESIS because the leaves of the desert plant are reduced to SPINES to cut down water loss (transpiration). Thus a plant like Opuntia can both make food (through the green stem) and conserve water (through spiny leaves) in dry conditions.
questions.explanation: Green stem photosynthesises while spiny leaves save water.

questions.question: Name the three parts of a typical dicot leaf.
questions.answer: A typical dicot leaf has a LEAF BASE (attaching it to the stem), a PETIOLE (the stalk) and a LAMINA (the broad green blade). Small stipules may be present at the leaf base.
questions.explanation: Leaf base, petiole, lamina.

questions.question: Distinguish between a simple leaf and a compound leaf.
questions.answer: In a SIMPLE leaf the lamina is undivided, or if incised the cuts do not reach the midrib (e.g. mango). In a COMPOUND leaf the lamina is completely divided into separate LEAFLETS, the incisions reaching down to the midrib or petiole (e.g. neem). A bud lies in the axil of a whole leaf but not in the axil of a leaflet.
questions.explanation: Simple = undivided; compound = divided into leaflets.

questions.question: What is phyllotaxy? Name its three types.
questions.answer: PHYLLOTAXY is the pattern of arrangement of leaves on the stem or branch, arranged so that each leaf gets maximum light. Its three types are ALTERNATE (one leaf per node), OPPOSITE (a pair per node) and WHORLED (more than two per node).
questions.explanation: Arrangement of leaves; alternate, opposite, whorled.

questions.question: Describe the mesophyll of a dorsiventral leaf.
questions.answer: The MESOPHYLL is the green tissue between the two epidermal layers, differentiated into two regions: the PALISADE PARENCHYMA (long, closely packed, chloroplast-rich cells just below the upper epidermis, doing most photosynthesis) and the SPONGY PARENCHYMA (loose cells with large air spaces towards the lower epidermis, allowing gas diffusion).
questions.explanation: Palisade (upper, photosynthesis) + spongy (lower, air spaces).

questions.question: What are stomata and what is their function?
questions.answer: STOMATA are tiny pores in the epidermis of the leaf, each bordered by two GUARD CELLS. They open and close to control the EXCHANGE OF GASES (carbon dioxide in, oxygen out during photosynthesis) and the loss of water vapour (TRANSPIRATION).
questions.explanation: Pores with guard cells; control gas exchange and transpiration.

questions.question: Give three differences between a dorsiventral leaf and an isobilateral leaf.
questions.answer: (1) The MESOPHYLL is differentiated into palisade and spongy layers in a dorsiventral leaf but is UNIFORM in an isobilateral leaf. (2) STOMATA are more numerous on the lower surface in a dorsiventral leaf but occur about EQUALLY on both surfaces in an isobilateral leaf. (3) The dorsiventral leaf has distinct upper and lower surfaces (and a thicker upper cuticle), whereas the isobilateral leaf has both surfaces alike and often bears bulliform cells.
questions.explanation: Differentiated vs uniform mesophyll; stomata below vs both sides; distinct vs alike surfaces.

questions.question: Describe any three modifications of the leaf with one example each.
questions.answer: (1) LEAF TENDRIL - the leaf or leaflet becomes a thin coiling tendril for climbing (e.g. pea). (2) LEAF SPINE - leaves become hard pointed spines that reduce water loss and give protection (e.g. Opuntia). (3) INSECT-CATCHING LEAF - the leaf forms a trap to catch and digest insects for nitrogen (e.g. the pitcher of Nepenthes). Fleshy storage leaves (onion) are a further example.
questions.explanation: Tendril (pea), spine (Opuntia), insect trap (Nepenthes).

questions.question: Explain how the structure of a leaf is suited to photosynthesis.
questions.answer: The leaf is well suited to photosynthesis because: its broad, flat LAMINA offers a large surface to catch sunlight and carbon dioxide; it is THIN so light and gases reach the inner cells easily; the mesophyll cells (especially palisade) are packed with CHLOROPLASTS that trap light; numerous STOMATA allow carbon dioxide to enter and oxygen to leave; and a network of VEINS brings water to the cells and carries away the food made.
questions.explanation: Broad thin lamina, chloroplasts, stomata and veins suit photosynthesis.

questions.question: Describe the external features and functions of the stem.
questions.answer:
EXTERNAL FEATURES: The stem is the ascending axis of the plant that develops from the plumule. It bears NODES (points from which leaves arise) and INTERNODES (regions between nodes). At each node one or more leaves are borne, and in the axil of each leaf lies an AXILLARY bud; a TERMINAL bud sits at the tip. Young stems are green and photosynthetic, become woody with age, and grow upward towards light (positively phototropic) and against gravity (negatively geotropic). The stem branches to spread the leaves for maximum light.
FUNCTIONS: (1) SUPPORT - it holds up the leaves, flowers and fruits and displays them to light and pollinators. (2) CONDUCTION - the xylem carries water and minerals upward from the roots to the leaves, and the phloem carries the food made in the leaves to all parts of the plant. (3) PHOTOSYNTHESIS - young green stems make food. (4) STORAGE - some stems store food and water. (5) VEGETATIVE PROPAGATION and other special jobs (climbing, protection) through modified stems.
questions.explanation: External: nodes, internodes, buds, upward growth. Functions: support, conduction, photosynthesis, storage, propagation.

questions.question: With reference to a transverse section, describe the internal structure of a young dicot stem.
questions.answer:
A transverse section of a young dicot stem shows the following zones from outside inwards:
(1) EPIDERMIS - the outermost single layer of cells with a waterproof cuticle, a few stomata and sometimes hairs; it protects and checks water loss.
(2) HYPODERMIS - a few layers of COLLENCHYMA below the epidermis giving mechanical strength to the young green stem.
(3) CORTEX - several layers of parenchyma; the outer cells may photosynthesise and store food.
(4) ENDODERMIS - the innermost cortical layer, rich in starch, hence the STARCH SHEATH.
(5) PERICYCLE - sclerenchyma (with parenchyma) inside the endodermis, capping the bundles.
(6) VASCULAR BUNDLES - arranged in a RING around the pith; each is conjoint, collateral and OPEN (cambium between xylem and phloem), with phloem outside and xylem inside, so the stem can undergo secondary growth.
(7) PITH - the large central parenchyma that stores food and water; strips of pith between bundles are the MEDULLARY RAYS.
questions.explanation: Epidermis, hypodermis, cortex, endodermis, pericycle, ring of open bundles, pith.

questions.question: Compare the internal structure of a dicot stem and a monocot stem under suitable headings.
questions.answer:
1. HYPODERMIS: collenchymatous in the dicot stem; sclerenchymatous in the monocot stem.
2. GROUND TISSUE: the dicot stem is clearly zoned into cortex, endodermis (starch sheath), pericycle and central pith; the monocot stem has a continuous, undifferentiated ground tissue.
3. VASCULAR BUNDLE ARRANGEMENT: bundles in a RING in the dicot stem; SCATTERED in the ground tissue in the monocot stem.
4. TYPE OF BUNDLE: both are conjoint and collateral (phloem outside, xylem inside), but dicot bundles are OPEN (with cambium) while monocot bundles are CLOSED (no cambium) and are surrounded by a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath, often with a water cavity in the xylem.
5. SECONDARY GROWTH: present in the dicot stem (because of cambium); absent or negligible in the monocot stem.
6. PITH: distinct in the dicot stem; not distinct (part of ground tissue) in the monocot stem.
questions.explanation: Hypodermis, zonation, arrangement, open vs closed bundles, secondary growth, pith.

questions.question: Classify stem modifications into three groups and describe each with examples.
questions.answer:
Stem modifications are grouped as underground, sub-aerial and aerial.
(A) UNDERGROUND (storage and perennation): RHIZOME - a horizontal underground stem with nodes, scale leaves and buds (ginger); STEM TUBER - the swollen tip of an underground branch whose eyes are nodes with buds (potato); BULB - a reduced disc-like stem with fleshy scale leaves (onion); CORM - a short swollen vertical underground stem (Colocasia).
(B) SUB-AERIAL (vegetative propagation): RUNNER - creeps and roots at nodes (grass); STOLON - a branch that arches to the soil and roots (strawberry); OFFSET - a short thick horizontal branch giving a rosette (water hyacinth); SUCKER - grows below the soil then emerges as a new shoot (mint).
(C) AERIAL (special functions): STEM TENDRIL - a thin coiling branch for climbing (grapevine); THORN - a hard pointed branch for protection (Citrus); PHYLLOCLADE - a green photosynthetic stem of xerophytes with spiny leaves (Opuntia). In every case the structure keeps stem features (nodes, internodes, buds, scale leaves).
questions.explanation: Underground (rhizome, tuber, bulb, corm), sub-aerial (runner, stolon, offset, sucker), aerial (tendril, thorn, phylloclade).

questions.question: Describe the external structure of a leaf, including its parts, venation, types and phyllotaxy.
questions.answer:
PARTS: A typical leaf has a LEAF BASE (attaching it to the stem, sometimes a sheath or pulvinus), a PETIOLE (the stalk holding the blade to the light) and a LAMINA (the broad green blade with a midrib, veins and veinlets). Stipules may occur at the leaf base.
VENATION: The arrangement of veins is RETICULATE (net-like, typical of dicots, e.g. mango) or PARALLEL (veins parallel, typical of monocots, e.g. grass).
TYPES: A SIMPLE leaf has an undivided lamina (mango); a COMPOUND leaf is divided into leaflets - pinnate (leaflets on a rachis, e.g. neem) or palmate (leaflets from a common point, e.g. silk cotton). A bud lies in the axil of the whole leaf, not of a leaflet.
PHYLLOTAXY: The arrangement of leaves may be ALTERNATE (one per node, e.g. China rose), OPPOSITE (a pair per node, e.g. guava/Calotropis) or WHORLED (more than two per node, e.g. Nerium), arranged so each leaf gets maximum sunlight.
questions.explanation: Parts (base, petiole, lamina); venation; simple/compound; phyllotaxy.

questions.question: Draw and describe (in words) the internal structure of a dorsiventral leaf.
questions.answer:
A vertical section of a dorsiventral leaf shows three tissue systems.
(1) EPIDERMIS: a single layer on both surfaces covered by a cuticle. The UPPER epidermis has a thicker cuticle and fewer stomata; the LOWER epidermis has more stomata, each guarded by two guard cells. The epidermis protects and reduces water loss.
(2) MESOPHYLL: the green tissue between the epidermal layers, differentiated into (a) PALISADE PARENCHYMA - long, closely packed, chloroplast-rich cells just below the upper epidermis that carry out most photosynthesis; and (b) SPONGY PARENCHYMA - loosely arranged cells with large intercellular air spaces towards the lower epidermis that allow gases to diffuse to and from the stomata.
(3) VASCULAR BUNDLES: present in the veins, conjoint, collateral and closed, with XYLEM towards the upper side and PHLOEM towards the lower side, each surrounded by a parenchymatous bundle sheath. Xylem brings water, phloem removes the food made in the leaf.
questions.explanation: Epidermis (both sides, guard cells), palisade + spongy mesophyll, closed vascular bundles.

questions.question: Compare the internal structure of a dorsiventral (dicot) leaf with that of an isobilateral (monocot) leaf.
questions.answer:
1. SURFACES: the DORSIVENTRAL leaf has distinct upper and lower surfaces; the ISOBILATERAL leaf has both surfaces alike.
2. CUTICLE: the upper cuticle is thicker in the dorsiventral leaf; both cuticles are about equal in the isobilateral leaf.
3. STOMATA: more numerous on the LOWER surface in the dorsiventral leaf; about EQUAL on both surfaces in the isobilateral leaf.
4. MESOPHYLL: DIFFERENTIATED into palisade (upper) and spongy (lower) in the dorsiventral leaf; UNIFORM (undifferentiated) in the isobilateral leaf.
5. BULLIFORM CELLS: absent in the dorsiventral leaf; present (in the upper epidermis of grasses) in the isobilateral leaf, helping to fold the leaf and reduce water loss.
6. VASCULAR BUNDLES: in both, conjoint, collateral and closed with a bundle sheath, but arranged along net-like veins in the dorsiventral leaf and along parallel veins of varying size in the isobilateral leaf.
questions.explanation: Surfaces, cuticle, stomata, mesophyll, bulliform cells, vein pattern.

questions.question: Describe the modifications and functions of the leaf.
questions.answer:
MODIFICATIONS: (1) LEAF TENDRILS - the whole leaf or leaflets become thin coiling tendrils for climbing (pea, Lathyrus). (2) LEAF SPINES - leaves reduced to hard pointed spines that cut water loss and protect the plant (Opuntia). (3) STORAGE (fleshy) LEAVES - thick leaves that store food and water (onion scales, Aloe). (4) INSECT-CATCHING LEAVES - traps that catch and digest insects for nitrogen in poor soils (pitcher of Nepenthes, Venus flytrap). Some plants (Bryophyllum) even bear buds on the leaf margin for propagation.
FUNCTIONS: (1) PHOTOSYNTHESIS - the leaf is the main organ that makes food using sunlight, carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen. (2) TRANSPIRATION - loss of water vapour through the stomata, which cools the leaf and pulls water up from the roots. (3) GASEOUS EXCHANGE - intake of carbon dioxide and release of oxygen through stomata. (4) Special jobs by modified leaves - storage, climbing, protection, trapping insects and vegetative propagation.
questions.explanation: Modifications: tendril, spine, storage, insect trap. Functions: photosynthesis, transpiration, gas exchange, special jobs.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A gardener notices that a green climbing shoot bears small leaves at regular points, and in the angle between each leaf and the stem there is a tiny bud. The tip of the shoot keeps growing longer.
(a) What is the point where each leaf arises called?
(b) What is the bud in the leaf angle called and what does it form?
(c) What is the bud at the growing tip called and what is its role?
(d) Give one reason why this structure is a stem and not a root.
questions.answer:
(a) The point where each leaf arises is a NODE.
(b) The bud in the angle (axil) between the leaf and the stem is an AXILLARY (lateral) bud; it grows into a branch or a flower.
(c) The bud at the growing tip is the TERMINAL (apical) bud; it is responsible for growth in length of the shoot.
(d) It bears nodes, internodes and buds (and leaves), which roots never have - so it is a stem.
questions.explanation: Node, axillary bud (branch/flower), terminal bud (length), nodes/buds prove stem.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A transverse section of a young sunflower stem shows, from outside inwards, a cuticle-covered outer layer, a few layers of thick-cornered cells, a broad parenchyma zone, a starch-rich inner layer, and vascular bundles arranged in a ring around a large central region.
(a) Name the outer layer and one function.
(b) Name the thick-cornered layer and its tissue.
(c) What is the starch-rich inner layer called?
(d) Name the central region and the bundle arrangement.
questions.answer:
(a) The outer layer is the EPIDERMIS; it protects the inner tissues and (with its cuticle) reduces water loss.
(b) The thick-cornered layer is the HYPODERMIS, made of COLLENCHYMA.
(c) The starch-rich inner layer is the ENDODERMIS (starch sheath).
(d) The central region is the PITH, and the vascular bundles are arranged in a RING (typical of a dicot stem).
questions.explanation: Epidermis, collenchyma hypodermis, endodermis (starch sheath), pith with ring of bundles.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Two stem sections are examined. In section X the vascular bundles are scattered throughout a continuous ground tissue and each has a sclerenchyma sheath; in section Y the bundles lie in a ring and each has a strip of cambium between xylem and phloem.
(a) Which section is a monocot and which is a dicot?
(b) Which section can undergo secondary growth and why?
(c) Are the bundles of X open or closed?
(d) Name one feature common to the bundles of both X and Y.
questions.answer:
(a) Section X (scattered bundles) is a MONOCOT stem; section Y (ring of bundles with cambium) is a DICOT stem.
(b) Section Y (the dicot) can undergo SECONDARY GROWTH because its bundles are OPEN - the cambium divides and adds new xylem and phloem, increasing girth.
(c) The bundles of X are CLOSED (no cambium).
(d) In both X and Y the bundles are CONJOINT and COLLATERAL, with phloem on the outer side and xylem on the inner side.
questions.explanation: X monocot, Y dicot; Y secondary growth (open/cambium); X closed; both conjoint-collateral.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A student examines four food-storing plant parts: a potato with 'eyes', an onion made of fleshy scales, a horizontal ginger with scale leaves and buds, and a strawberry plant sending out a branch that arches to the soil and forms a new plant.
(a) What kind of modified stem is the potato and what are its eyes?
(b) Name the modification seen in the onion.
(c) Name the ginger modification.
(d) Name the strawberry modification and its function.
questions.answer:
(a) The potato is a STEM TUBER; its 'eyes' are NODES bearing axillary buds.
(b) The onion is a BULB (a reduced stem with fleshy storage scale leaves).
(c) The ginger is a RHIZOME (a horizontal underground stem).
(d) The strawberry's arching branch is a STOLON, which serves in vegetative propagation (forming new plants).
questions.explanation: Potato = stem tuber (eyes = nodes); onion = bulb; ginger = rhizome; strawberry = stolon (propagation).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A leaf has a broad blade attached to the stem by a stalk. Its veins form a net-like pattern. Another plant's leaf is long and narrow with veins running parallel, and a single leaf arises at each node.
(a) Name the stalk of the first leaf.
(b) Name the venation of the first leaf and the plant group it suggests.
(c) Name the venation of the second leaf and its plant group.
(d) Name the phyllotaxy where one leaf arises at each node.
questions.answer:
(a) The stalk of the leaf is the PETIOLE.
(b) The first leaf shows RETICULATE (net-like) venation, suggesting a DICOT.
(c) The second leaf shows PARALLEL venation, suggesting a MONOCOT.
(d) When one leaf arises at each node the phyllotaxy is ALTERNATE.
questions.explanation: Petiole; reticulate (dicot); parallel (monocot); alternate phyllotaxy.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A vertical section of a dicot leaf shows an upper epidermis with a thick cuticle, then long cylindrical chloroplast-rich cells, then loose cells with big air spaces, and a lower epidermis with many pores each between two special cells.
(a) Name the long cylindrical cells and their main job.
(b) Name the loose cells with air spaces and their role.
(c) Name the pores and the two cells guarding each.
(d) On which surface are the pores more numerous here?
questions.answer:
(a) The long cylindrical chloroplast-rich cells are the PALISADE PARENCHYMA; they carry out most of the photosynthesis.
(b) The loose cells with air spaces are the SPONGY PARENCHYMA; they allow gases to diffuse to and from the stomata.
(c) The pores are STOMATA, each guarded by two GUARD CELLS.
(d) The pores (stomata) are more numerous on the LOWER surface.
questions.explanation: Palisade (photosynthesis), spongy (gas diffusion), stomata + guard cells, more below.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Two leaf sections are compared. Leaf P has an upper palisade layer and a lower spongy layer, with most stomata on the lower surface. Leaf Q has a uniform mesophyll, stomata equally on both surfaces, and large thin-walled cells in the upper epidermis.
(a) Which leaf is dorsiventral and which is isobilateral?
(b) How do their mesophylls differ?
(c) What are the large thin-walled cells in leaf Q and their function?
(d) State one feature common to the vascular bundles of both leaves.
questions.answer:
(a) Leaf P is DORSIVENTRAL (dicot); leaf Q is ISOBILATERAL (monocot).
(b) Leaf P has a DIFFERENTIATED mesophyll (palisade above, spongy below), whereas leaf Q has a UNIFORM (undifferentiated) mesophyll.
(c) The large thin-walled cells in leaf Q are BULLIFORM (motor) cells; they lose water and fold/roll the leaf during dryness to reduce transpiration.
(d) In both leaves the vascular bundles are CONJOINT, COLLATERAL and CLOSED, each with a bundle sheath.
questions.explanation: P dorsiventral, Q isobilateral; differentiated vs uniform mesophyll; bulliform cells; conjoint-collateral-closed bundles.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
In a desert, a cactus has no broad leaves - its leaves are hard spines while its flat green stem makes food. In a nearby marsh, a pitcher plant catches and digests insects using a modified leaf, because the soil is poor in nitrogen.
(a) Into what are the cactus leaves modified and why?
(b) What is the green food-making stem of the cactus called?
(c) What is the insect-trapping structure of the pitcher plant a modification of?
(d) Why does the pitcher plant trap insects?
questions.answer:
(a) The cactus leaves are modified into SPINES to reduce water loss (transpiration) in the dry desert and to give protection.
(b) The green flattened food-making stem is a PHYLLOCLADE, which takes over photosynthesis.
(c) The insect-trapping pitcher is a modification of a LEAF.
(d) The pitcher plant traps and digests insects to obtain NITROGEN, which is scarce in the marshy soil.
questions.explanation: Leaves to spines (save water); phylloclade photosynthesises; pitcher = modified leaf; traps insects for nitrogen.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A piece of underground ginger looks like a root but bears tiny scale leaves, small buds and clear rings marking joints. When planted, buds sprout into new shoots.
(a) Name the joints where scale leaves and buds occur.
(b) Give two stem features seen in this ginger.
(c) Why can it grow into new shoots?
(d) Is it a stem or a root? Justify.
questions.answer:
(a) The joints are NODES; the regions between them are internodes.
(b) Two stem features are: (i) the presence of NODES and INTERNODES, and (ii) SCALE LEAVES with BUDS in their axils.
(c) It can grow into new shoots because its buds are undeveloped shoots that sprout - buds occur only on stems.
(d) It is a STEM (a rhizome), because roots never bear nodes, scale leaves or buds.
questions.explanation: Nodes; nodes/internodes + scale leaves with buds; buds sprout; a stem (rhizome).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A neem leaf is divided into many small leaflets along a central axis, yet a single bud is seen only at the base where the whole structure joins the stem, not at the base of any leaflet. A mango leaf beside it is a single undivided blade.
(a) Is the neem leaf simple or compound? What kind?
(b) Is the mango leaf simple or compound?
(c) How does the position of the bud prove the neem structure is one leaf, not a branch?
(d) What are the small divisions of the neem leaf called?
questions.answer:
(a) The neem leaf is COMPOUND; because its leaflets lie along a central axis (rachis) it is PINNATELY compound.
(b) The mango leaf is a SIMPLE leaf (undivided blade).
(c) A bud lies in the axil of a WHOLE leaf but never in the axil of a leaflet. Since the bud is only at the base of the whole neem structure and not at the base of any leaflet, the structure is a single (compound) leaf, not a branch bearing simple leaves.
(d) The small divisions are called LEAFLETS.
questions.explanation: Neem = pinnately compound; mango = simple; bud only at whole-leaf base; divisions = leaflets.
